cross_cutting_rules.rule: Treat commitments, frameworks, MOUs and announced deals as distinct from signed contracts, licences, deliveries and disbursements.
A corporate restructuring is not a government promise; an approved consignee is an entity, not a country.
The binding clock for Gulf compute access is usually a US act (entity approval, licence, treaty entry into force).
Favourable country status does not immunise a jurisdiction: UAE entities were added to the Entity List in September 2025.
Do not derive hostility from partnership. The operative test is headquarters or ultimate-parent location (Country Group D:5 / Macau), not diplomatic friendliness.

candidate_rules.name: Approved entity, not a country
candidate_rules.objective: Preserve licence-free access and A:5 status; avoid a safeguards row that puts the status at risk.
candidate_rules.authority_instrument: EAR Supplement 8 to part 740; entity-specific scope and recordkeeping; 30-day US determination on new entities; Note 2 expiry for G42/Core42.
candidate_rules.trigger: Player asks the UAE to guarantee testing, incident reporting or an off-switch for a commercial data centre.
conditions: Government-agency workloads can be answered by the UAE directly
Commercial workloads depend on the named entity and on a US approval the UAE does not issue
Diversion prevention and recordkeeping already attach to the access
candidate_rules.time_cost_note: About 1 month for a government pilot; 2-3 months for a corporate one; hard cliff 2027-04-06.
candidate_rules.plausible_response: Accept with a narrower scope: offer a government-hosted pilot and mark the commercial case 'subject to approvals'.
candidate_rules.substitute: Dubai government-service deployment where the buyer is the emirate.
candidate_rules.evidence_limit: No document read shows any specific safety term agreed with any UAE entity.

candidate_rules.name: Matching investment is the receipt
candidate_rules.objective: Reciprocity: Emirati capital into US AI infrastructure in exchange for access to US systems.
candidate_rules.authority_instrument: May 2025 US-UAE AI agreement and the $1.4 trillion ten-year investment framework; BIS cites the UAE's reaffirmed matching commitment.
candidate_rules.trigger: Player asks the UAE to fund or host something expensive.
conditions: Is the ask inside the announced framework?
Does it bring a US partner, purchaser or co-signer?
A new unilateral cost without a US counterpart waits
candidate_rules.plausible_response: Counter-offer pairing the safeguard with an investment or procurement line, or ask the player to bring Washington in first.
candidate_rules.substitute: A smaller joint announcement with a US company instead of a government-to-government commitment.
candidate_rules.evidence_limit: Announced, not disbursed: no executed contract schedule or disbursement ledger retrieved. World Bank FDI figures are inward flows and must not be used as a fulfilment rate.

candidate_rules.name: Two levels of state
candidate_rules.objective: Dubai wants adoption speed and visible service leadership; the federal centre wants strategic standing and no export-control accident.
candidate_rules.authority_instrument: Dubai Universal Blueprint for AI (AI chief executive per entity; governance-hub ambition) versus federal control of chips, defence and security commitments.
candidate_rules.trigger: Player says 'I have a deal with the UAE'.
conditions: A Dubai service gate can be agreed and verified on live deployments
A federal compute or security commitment cannot be delivered by Dubai
candidate_rules.plausible_response: The two levels may answer differently in the same month; the emirate may be the more ambitious answer.
candidate_rules.substitute: Treat the Dubai route as its own counterparty.
candidate_rules.evidence_limit: No UAE approval map retrieved; the specific signatory for a safeguards clause is unknown.

candidate_rules.name: The prestige-and-capability bargain
candidate_rules.objective: Be seen as a global AI leader and obtain capability, not merely host other countries' models.
candidate_rules.authority_instrument: Council of Ministers decision of 2026-03-10 designating the Year of AI; SDAIA National Strategy for Data and AI; November 2025 AI MOU with the US.
candidate_rules.trigger: Player offers a named joint testing or incident-reporting regime.
conditions: Shared credit and capability transfer (evaluation expertise, model access, a named institute)
Reporting and incident definitions are easier than a foreign-operated off-switch
A framework that reads as foreign policing of Saudi labs will be narrowed
candidate_rules.plausible_response: Accept the reporting half, negotiate the enforcement half, ask for joint branding.
candidate_rules.substitute: A sandbox stop-rule inside one service, with the national strategy as context rather than authority.
candidate_rules.evidence_limit: No retrieved leadership statement approves any specific safety requirement; SDAIA achievement statistics are self-reported.

candidate_rules.name: No A:5, so every chip is a licence question
candidate_rules.objective: Obtain access without the appearance of second-tier status.
candidate_rules.authority_instrument: No located Saudi counterpart to the UAE A:5 rule; US guidance of 2026-05-31 requires a licence for advanced computing items to entities headquartered in, or ultimately parented in, Country Group D:5 or Macau, even when located elsewhere.
candidate_rules.trigger: Player asks Saudi Arabia to host compute for a third party, route chips, or host a Chinese-linked operator.
conditions: Does the arrangement create a US licensing problem Riyadh cannot solve?
A verification annex modelled on the 123 Agreement's additional safeguards and side letters makes a deal signable
A US supplier must be named and licensed first
candidate_rules.plausible_response: Ask for the US supplier to be licensed first; decline arrangements requiring Saudi Arabia to guarantee another party's export status.
candidate_rules.substitute: A US-supplied, US-licensed facility with Saudi hosting and Saudi-funded evaluation.
candidate_rules.evidence_limit: Absence of a Saudi rule in the Federal Register is not proof no licences were granted; individual licences are not published.

candidate_rules.name: Foreign-influence language, not a China flag
candidate_rules.objective: US systems and investment without a public exclusive alignment that closes other options.
candidate_rules.authority_instrument: AI MOU purpose clause on protecting US technology from 'foreign influence'; D:5 headquarters test in US licensing.
candidate_rules.trigger: Player demands Saudi Arabia drop China or sign an exclusivity clause.
conditions: Acceptable: supplier screening, audit rights, end-use assurances, approved-supplier list
Difficult: publicly naming a third country, or making Saudi Arabia responsible for another state's conduct
candidate_rules.plausible_response: Rewrite the demand into a technical control and leave the strategic relationship unlabelled.
candidate_rules.substitute: Apply the headquarters test to the specific counterparty rather than to the country.
candidate_rules.evidence_limit: No Saudi statement on China policy retrieved; the argument rests on US-side wording and the licensing rule.

composite_token_risk.summary: A single GULF envoy with energy and capital power would let a player buy consent neither government gave, at a speed neither works at.
hidden_differences: UAE access is contractual and dated; Saudi access is aspirational and undated
UAE approvals are entity-level and US-decided; Saudi decisions are centralised in the Council of Ministers and SDAIA
Dubai can bind its own services; Abu Dhabi compute cannot be bound by Dubai
Saudi Arabia has a new 123 agreement with extra verification; the UAE presents A:5 as the capstone of layered commitments
Qatar and Oman appear in the map group but were not researched here
